name: Zane Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the shearer on the longwall at the Blackwater underground coal mine, have done for twenty-two years. The shearer's the big cutting machine that runs back and forth along the coal face, and I'm the one steering the drums and keeping the face straight. Day shift means I'm in the cage by six, and by half past I'm checking picks and water sprays with my offsider, Kip, who's twenty-four and still learning. I love the moment the face is running clean and you can hear it in the machine, but the dust and the noise wear on your body by the end of the week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else is part of the job besides running the machine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the union delegate for our crew, so half my lunch break goes on somebody's roster problem or a safety complaint. I also teach the young ones to read the roof, because no screen tells you when the ground's about to talk. My wife Rita cooks at the primary school, and our two kids are grown and gone, Daniel nursing in the city and Sofia teaching. Seven more years and I'm out with a pension, if my knees hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying in the crib room for years: they promised us robots and we got a new tablet for the pre-start checklist. The company would still need men and women on the face. I'd probably post a photo of that tablet with a crack across the screen and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I get to finish my seven years the way I started them. That's what I want. I don't use any of these AI things, and if I never have to, I'll be glad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep turning up, keep training Kip, and keep pushing the company on the dust levels at the next safety meeting in March. Rita and I would keep putting a bit aside each month like we already do, which isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. A bit of me would also feel smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said smug. Who would you feel smug towards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The suits at head office who keep showing us slides about the mine of the future. Every few years there's a new consultant, a new word, and the coal still has to be cut by someone who knows what he's doing. I've seen three of those programs come and go since 2004.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company would still use any excuse to cut a shift. Even small savings from AI, they'd take it out of our hides, not out of the bonus pool upstairs. So I'd still be watching the next enterprise agreement like a hawk.

S0.say: They promised us robots and we got a new tablet for the pre-start checklist. The company still needs skilled people on the face, same as ever.
S0.think: This means I get to finish my last seven years the way I started them. I don't use any of these AI things, and I'd be glad never to have to.
S0.do: Keeps working the longwall and training his offsider Kip as normal. Keeps pressing the company on dust levels and keeps putting a small amount aside each month with Rita.
S0.feel: Relieved, with a touch of smugness towards head office.
S0.quote: They promised us robots and we got a new tablet for the pre-start checklist.
S0.fieldNote: Zane is settled in his trade and his union role, and this picture simply confirms what he already believes about hype. His one live worry is that management would use even small savings to trim shifts. Distrust of head office runs underneath everything he says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union says: if the work changes, the workers get a say in how. No new system on the face without proper consultation and training on company time. I'd be the one standing up at the lodge meeting saying that out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not the person who learns a new screen fast. If they bring in remote shearer control from the surface, someone like Kip will pick it up in a week and I'll be fumbling. I'd still have the know-how of the ground, but I'm not sure they'd value that once the cameras are in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd make sure our next agreement had a clause about retraining and no forced redundancies for anyone over fifty-five. I'd keep doing my shifts and I'd go to whatever training they offered, even if I hated it. And I'd sit down with Rita and work out whether we could pay off the last four years of the mortgage early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like walking into a new section where you don't know the roof yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture the first day they put you in a surface control room. What happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit there with a coffee and six screens, and I'd miss the smell of the face. I'd probably ring Kip on the radio every ten minutes asking what the pick wear looks like. The machine would be cutting coal and I'd feel like a passenger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try to pay off the mortgage early. Where does that money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the trip to see Daniel every Easter, that's the honest answer. Probably also skip the new ute and keep patching the old one. It's not much money, but four years is four years.

S1.say: If the work changes, the workers get a say in how. No new system goes on the face without proper consultation and training on company time.
S1.think: I'm not the person who learns a new screen fast, and Kip would pick up remote control in a week while I fumble. I'd still know the ground, but I'm not sure they'd value that once the cameras are in.
S1.do: Pushes for a retraining clause and no forced redundancies over fifty-five in the next agreement. Attends whatever training is offered and looks at paying off the last four years of the mortgage early by skipping trips and a new vehicle.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like being in a new section where he doesn't yet know the roof.
S1.quote: I'd sit there with a coffee and six screens, and I'd miss the smell of the face.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is firm union language, but in private he admits he is slow with new technology and fears being outpaced by his own trainee. The control room image clearly hurt him more than the money talk. He still expects to have a job here, which keeps him from real fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd be saying the companies and their shareholders are going to pocket the lot, and the government's asleep. I'd be at every rally the union called, and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'd be sixty in 2028 with about three months of savings and five years short of the pension. If a robot can run the longwall and another one can do the maintenance, there's no job for me anywhere, not here and not at the other mines down the valley. That's the bit I can't get past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut everything we don't need, the car upgrade, eating out, the lot, and put every spare dollar into savings. I'd push the union to fight for a bridging payment to the pension for anyone over fifty-five. If it came to it, I'd talk to Sofia and Daniel about whether we might need help, which would kill me to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in the stomach, if I'm honest. I'd be lying awake doing sums at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rita the night you heard the mine was going fully robotic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we'd been through the 2012 layoffs and we'd get through this. But she'd see straight through me, she always does. Then we'd probably sit at the kitchen table and go through the bank statements line by line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, no question, there's still four years on it. After that the health insurance, because my back and knees are going to need work whether I'm employed or not. Power and food we'd manage somehow.

S2.say: The companies and their shareholders are going to pocket the lot, and the government is asleep. I'd be at every rally the union called and saying it to anyone at the pub.
S2.think: I'd be sixty with about three months of savings and five years short of the pension. If robots do the cutting and the maintenance, there's no job for me anywhere in the valley.
S2.do: Cuts all non-essential spending at once and saves every spare dollar. Pushes the union for a bridging payment to the pension for workers over fifty-five, and would ask his grown children for help if needed.
S2.feel: Sick in the stomach and losing sleep over the numbers.
S2.quote: I'd tell her we'd been through the 2012 layoffs and we'd get through this. But she'd see straight through me, she always does.
S2.fieldNote: Two years is far too short for Zane: he lands in the gap between losing work and reaching his pension. His anger at shareholders and government is real, but the private fear is about the mortgage and his body. Asking his children for help is clearly the thing he dreads most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government or the company to be caught napping. I'd want laws on the books before the robots are in the pit. That would be my line in every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2031 puts me at sixty-three. That's close enough to the pension that I might just scrape through, or I might get pushed out two years short. It's a coin toss, and I don't like coin tosses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to pay the mortgage down hard and build the savings from three months to maybe nine. I'd work every overtime shift I could get while my knees allow. And I'd push the union to lobby for early access to the pension for miners displaced by machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have something to do with the worry. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said with the fast one, you'd be cutting back. What's different with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be panicking and cutting. With five I'd be planning. I could see the finish line from here, whereas in the fast one it's like the finish line gets moved further away while you're running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kip, mostly. He's got a baby on the way and he's put everything into this trade. I'd tell him to get his electrical ticket now while the company's still paying for training.

S3.say: We've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government or the company to be caught napping. I want laws on the books before the robots are in the pit.
S3.think: I'd be sixty-three in 2031, so I might scrape through to the pension or get pushed out two years short. It's a coin toss, and I don't like coin tosses.
S3.do: Pays the mortgage down hard and aims to grow savings from about three months to nine. Works every overtime shift his knees allow, and pushes the union to lobby for early pension access for displaced miners.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadier because the worry has a plan attached to it.
S3.quote: I could see the finish line from here, whereas in the fast one it's like the finish line gets moved further away while you're running.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years change Zane from panic to planning. He still sees real risk of losing work before his pension, but he can picture a route through it. His concern turns outward quickly to Kip, which says a lot about how he sees his role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where nobody can say they didn't see it coming. Ten years is plenty of time to retrain the young ones and look after the old ones. If governments mess this up, it's because they chose to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, I'm out by 2033, so I'd probably be on the pension before the robots arrive. It's not my job I'd worry about, it's the town. If the mine goes fully automatic, the pub and the footy club and the school where Rita works all shrink with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my shifts as normal until I retire. I'd spend my union time on a transition plan for the young crew, things like paid training and moving people into whatever new work comes. I'd also vote for whoever had a real plan for towns like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the town, and a bit guilty that I get to slip out the door before it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said guilty. Can you say more about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad worked forty years down the pit so I could have this job. I'd be the generation that got out just before the door shut. It feels like leaving a party right before the fight starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the young ones to stay in mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to stay while it pays, but to have a second trade in their back pocket. Electrical, plumbing, something where you go into people's houses. Though if robots can do that too by then, I honestly don't know what I'd tell them.

S4.say: This is the one where nobody can say they didn't see it coming. Ten years is plenty of time to retrain the young ones, and if governments mess it up, it's because they chose to.
S4.think: I'm out by 2033, so I'd probably be on the pension before the robots arrive. It's the town I'd worry about: the pub, the footy club and Rita's school all shrink with the mine.
S4.do: Keeps working his shifts as normal until retirement. Spends his union time on a transition plan for young workers and votes for whoever has a real plan for mining towns.
S4.feel: Uneasy for his town, and a little guilty that he gets out just before it hits.
S4.quote: My dad worked forty years down the pit so I could have this job. I'd be the generation that got out just before the door shut.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Zane is personally safe and knows it, so his worry becomes collective and moral. The guilt about slipping out ahead of the younger crew was unexpected and sincere. He admits he doesn't know what trade to recommend if robots reach everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no contest. Two years drops me in the hole between losing the job and getting the pension. What would help is a guaranteed bridge for people like me, so if the machines take the job at sixty, the pension or something like it starts at sixty too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the ground. A robot can cut coal, fine, but somebody has to decide what to do when the roof starts talking at three in the morning. I'd want to know who's responsible when a machine gets that wrong, because down there it's not a spreadsheet error, it's a funeral.

headlineQuote: Somebody has to decide what to do when the roof starts talking at three in the morning.
portrait: Zane Costa is a 58-year-old shearer operator on an underground coal longwall, a union delegate who trains the young crew and distrusts head office. He never uses AI and admits he would be slow to learn remote controls. He shrugs off the plateau, turns uneasy at steady change, and is alarmed by AGI in two years because it drops him five years short of his pension with a mortgage still running. With five or ten years his fear eases into planning, and his worry turns to his trainee Kip and the town around the mine.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would leave him without work at sixty and years short of his pension.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed bridge to the pension for workers who lose their jobs to machines, starting at the age the job ends.
